narration: This is Mongolian Tsam. 19th century introduction · Revived post-1991.
on_screen: Title card: Mongolian Tsam · Mongolia · 19th century introduction · Revived post-1991

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Tsam was not introduced to Mongolia until the early 19th century, quickly gaining popularity through celebrations and the opera Tale of the Moon Cuckoo.
It incorporated tantric and older shamanistic elements before being banned under communist rule in 1924 and severely impacted by the 1937 Stalinist purges.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed as a form of meditation and offering to the gods, offering moral instruction and bringing merit to observers.
Today it is a revived tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers wear elaborate costumes and carved masks.
Many masks and costumes survived Soviet purges by being buried, hidden, or stored in museums such as the Choijin Lama Temple Museum.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Practiced in Mongolia, Inner Mongolia, and Buryatia, sharing roots with Tibetan Cham and Bhutanese Tshechu performances.
Derived from the Tibetan Cham tradition, incorporating tantric and shamanistic elements upon its 19th-century introduction to Mongolia.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Tsam is a sacred Vajrayana Buddhist ritual dance performed by monks as an offering and meditation; outsiders must respect its religious context.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Mongolian Tsam (Mongolia). Instruments: traditional Tibetan musical instruments, cymbals. Mood: ritual, meditative, solemn. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
